paras: The lynching of Judy Metts took place on the night of April 9, 1881, when disguised horsemen took Metts, a Black woman accused of burning a barn, from a constable near Martin's Depot in Laurens County, South Carolina, and hanged her from a tree. A coroner's jury blamed persons unknown, and Governor Hagood offered $200 for each lyncher, but no arrests were reported. Because the victim was a woman accused of a property crime, several South Carolina papers called the killing murder and debated lynching for months.

On Sunday night, April 3, a barn belonging to J. S. Blalock at Martin's Depot burned, and because it stood near his dwelling, the fire was taken as an attempt on the house as well. Blalock concluded that the fire had been set by Judy Metts, who lived on his plantation and had been accused two years earlier of burning a Mr. Simpson's dwelling but never tried. The Newberry Herald gave her age as about thirty-five, with a husband and children, while a Newberry dispatch called her 'an old colored woman' named Eliza Cowan, alias Judith Metts.

On Saturday, April 9, Blalock obtained a warrant from Trial Justice N. S. Harris of Clinton, and Constable Samuel Gray (Sam'l Gary in the Newberry Herald) arrested Metts and started with her for Clinton about eight that night. About two miles above Martin's Depot, nearly opposite Henry M. Hunter's residence, horsemen with cloth over their faces overtook them; some held the constable while others carried the woman off. By the constable's own statement, he was kept about an hour, told to 'git,' and went on to Clinton.
The next morning Metts was found hanging dead from a tree about two hundred yards from the road, and after Monday's inquest she was buried by the colored people.

In a letter to the Laurensville Herald, the minister A. G. Leggette called the lynching a foul deed, asked why the arrest had been made at night, and wrote that 'the colored people are much excited and incensed.' In early May, after receiving the coroner's report, Governor Hagood offered $200 for the arrest and conviction of each of the twenty-five or thirty reported lynchers, about $6,000 in all. No arrest appears in the coverage, and in August the Abbeville Press and Banner reported a Laurens man's view that Black residents knew the lynchers but 'were afraid to inform against them.'

A Charleston telegram in the Richmond Dispatch on April 15 gave the first plain account. The Charleston News and Courier, copied by the Newberry Herald under the heading 'No Mob-Law in South Carolina,' declared that 'the lynching in Laurens was murder,' since house burning was already a capital crime. The Keowee Courier agreed that a barn fire did not call for lynching, though it allowed that rape and murder might excuse 'ultra legal remedies.'

The Abbeville Press and Banner condemned 'the habit of lynching weak and defenceless negroes' and printed a sarcastic mock defense of mob law beside the Legette letter and a New York Herald satire, 'Why Not Lynch Babies?' The Pickens Sentinel replied that the hanging 'can not be too severely condemned' but called the 'habit' charge unjust and warned that Northern 'bloody shirt organs' would quote it. Through the summer the Abbeville paper contrasted the inaction in Laurens with the prosecution of Black men for burning the Greenville opera house, and the Greenville News answered that the reward for 'the white men who murdered Judy Metts' exceeded what the State had done in its own case.

Outside the state, the Washington National Republican mocked the lynchers as 'Scions of Chivalry,' and the New Albany Weekly Review headed its brief 'A Dastardly Outrage.' Weeklies in Missouri, Minnesota, Nebraska and Wisconsin ran single lines in their crime columns.

Reports based on the inquest record gave about thirty lynchers, while the Abbeville Press and Banner later wrote of 'five, or six, or possibly eight, white men.' That paper once asserted the lynching happened 'in broad day light,' against the dispatches, and the Legette letter dated it to the 4th rather than the 9th. Some Northern briefs named the victim Ann Cowan, and one placed the lynching at Spartanburg.

reader.title: Lynching of Judy Metts
bases: Disguised mounted men took Judy Metts, a Black woman accused of barn-burning, from a constable and hanged her from a tree (A3, A12, A18).

A party of disguised horsemen, put at five to eight or at twenty-five to thirty, took an accused arsonist from a constable and hanged her, and a coroner's jury found she died 'at the hands of persons unknown' (A3, A12, A33, A41); the pretext was punishment for the barn fire (A3, A17).

The Charleston telegram, the News and Courier's Newberry dispatch, the Newberry Herald's local account and the Keowee Courier agree on the arrest, seizure, hanging and inquest verdict (A3, A10, A12, A18).

accounts.label: Charleston and Newberry dispatches (News and Courier)
accounts.gist: Masked horsemen overtook the constable two miles from Martin's Depot about 8 p.m. Saturday, held him an hour, and hanged the woman, found next morning 200 yards away.

accounts.label: Constable's statement
accounts.gist: He said part of the party kept him about an hour and then released him with the command to 'git', after which he went to Clinton.

accounts.label: Laurensville Herald letter (Legette)
accounts.gist: A poor half-witted woman suspected of burning an outhouse was taken from the constable 'last Saturday night, 4th inst.' and found hanging a few hours later; he asked why the arrest was made at night.

accounts.label: Abbeville Press and Banner
accounts.gist: It wrote that the lynching happened 'in broad day light' with only faces disguised, so the constable must have recognized voices; in July it put the lynchers at five to eight white men acting at night.

accounts.label: Reports on the inquest record
accounts.gist: The governor's information from the inquest put the lynchers at twenty-five or thirty.

framing.detail: The News and Courier, copied by the Newberry Herald, headed its piece 'No Mob-Law in South Carolina' and said 'The lynching in Laurens was murder'.
The Abbeville Press and Banner condemned 'the habit of lynching weak and defenceless negroes', ran a sarcastic mock defense of lynching, and kept pressing the case into August.
The Pickens Sentinel said the hanging 'can not be too severely condemned' but called the 'habit' charge unjust and listed earlier lynchings for rape and murder.
The Keowee Courier said lynching was never excusable yet allowed 'much allowance' where the crime was rape and murder, unlike a barn fire.
The National Republican mocked the 'Scions of Chivalry' and the New Albany Weekly Review headed its item 'A Dastardly Outrage'.
Western and Midwestern weeklies ran one-line briefs in crime columns.
A Massachusetts paper's jab at South Carolina's senators drew a retort from the New Haven Register about a Massachusetts shooting.

conflicts.note: One woman; the South Carolina local reports use Judy Metts.
The Legette letter's '4th' conflicts with the dated dispatches and the Newberry Herald; April 9, 1881 was the Saturday the warrant was served.

versions.value: night, after the constable started about 8 p.m.

conflicts.note: The detailed local accounts put it at night; the Abbeville paper's daylight claim is an editorial assertion, and the same paper later said 'in the night time'.
The larger figure was tied to the inquest report sent to the governor.
The Newberry Herald gave the local figure.
The Indiana brief alone names Spartanburg.
The Abbeville copy is evidently garbled.
